issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder and disposal of evidence may be sustained on the prosecution evidence viewed cumulatively where credible eyewitness accounts and corroborating evidence establish the core events beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: Several witnesses testified to seeing the deceased being assaulted and strangled by the accused.
Other witnesses testified to seeing the accused load bags containing body parts into a vehicle for disposal.
Medical evidence established that death resulted from strangulation and that the body parts belonged to one person.
Evidence also established a prior demand for money and threats, and recoveries included the deceased’s bicycle and items connected with the disposal of the body.
The court found that the evidence, taken as a whole, established the prosecution case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The evidence was sufficient to sustain the convictions, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In a circumstantial case, the circumstances relied on must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, and exclude every reasonable alternative hypothesis; suspicion cannot replace proof (Mousam Singha Roy v. State of W.B.). Evidence must be assessed cumulatively and in its entirety. Here, the case was not purely circumstantial because witnesses testified to the assault, strangulation, and disposal of the body.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and (credible_eyewitness_accounts or complete_circumstantial_chain) and evidence_corroborates_core_events and no_material_contradictions

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_accounts: Witnesses gave credible testimony about the accused’s involvement in the central events.
predicates.complete_circumstantial_chain: The prosecution established a complete chain of circumstances consistent with guilt and excluding reasonable alternatives.
predicates.evidence_corroborates_core_events: Independent evidence, such as medical or physical evidence, supported the account of the central events.
predicates.no_material_contradictions: The inconsistencies in the evidence did not materially undermine the prosecution’s account.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is appealed, credible eyewitness accounts or a complete circumstantial chain, supported on the core events and not materially contradicted, can result in the conviction being sustained.

issues.legal_issue: A hostile witness’s testimony may be relied on to the extent that it supports the prosecution case.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses did not fully support the prosecution case at trial.
The court found that other witnesses had independently proved the relevant facts and that portions of the hostile witnesses’ testimony also supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ hostile testimony did not undermine the prosecution case, and its supportive portions could be considered.
issues.legal_principle: A court may rely on the part of a hostile witness’s testimony that supports the prosecution case; the court applied Govindaraju @ Govinda v. State by Sriramapuram P.S. & Anr.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and witness_declared_hostile and testimony_partly_supports_prosecution and other_evidence_proves_relevant_facts

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution case in full and was treated as hostile.
predicates.testimony_partly_supports_prosecution: Part of the witness’s testimony supports the prosecution account.
predicates.other_evidence_proves_relevant_facts: Other evidence independently establishes the facts the witness was expected to prove.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, where a hostile witness partly supports the prosecution and other evidence proves the relevant facts, the supportive testimony may be relied on.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in examining witnesses, relationship to the victim, minor discrepancies, and investigative lapses do not by themselves require rejection of otherwise reliable prosecution evidence.
material_facts: Some witnesses were examined several days or weeks after the incident, and some witnesses were related to the deceased.
The investigating officer described investigative demands, including efforts to locate and arrest accused persons, and the court accepted the explanation for delay.
The court found the timing differences and variations in the witnesses’ accounts to be minor and not material to the core prosecution case.
The investigation had deficiencies, including failure to send certain items for forensic examination, but other evidence established the relevant facts.
issues.conclusion: The delays, relationships, minor discrepancies, and investigative deficiencies did not render the prosecution evidence unreliable or require acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: Delayed examination must be assessed in its circumstances, and a plausible explanation may be accepted (Banti alias Guddu v. State of M.P.; State of U.P. v. Satish). Related testimony requires careful evaluation, not mechanical rejection (Brathi alias Sukhdev Singh v. State of Punjab). An investigative defect alone is not a ground for acquittal (C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu; Sheo Shankar Singh v. State of Jharkhand). Under the explanation to Section 162 CrPC, an omission may amount to a contradiction if significant and relevant in context; whether it does so is a question of fact. Minor variations that do not affect the core case are not material contradictions (Sunil Kumar Sambhudayal Gupta v. State of Maharashtra; Subhash v. State of Haryana).

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and evidence_remains_credible_on_core_events and (delay_plausibly_explained or related_testimony_corroborated or discrepancies_are_minor or investigative_lapses_do_not_affect_core_proof)

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.evidence_remains_credible_on_core_events: The evidence remains credible on the events essential to the prosecution case.
predicates.delay_plausibly_explained: The circumstances provide a plausible explanation for the delay in examining witnesses.
predicates.related_testimony_corroborated: Testimony from people related to the victim is supported by other evidence.
predicates.discrepancies_are_minor: Differences in witness accounts do not materially undermine the core prosecution case.
predicates.investigative_lapses_do_not_affect_core_: Investigative deficiencies do not undermine proof of the central facts.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, evidence is not rejected merely for delay, witness relationships, minor discrepancies, or investigative lapses when the core evidence remains credible and the relevant deficiency is explained, corroborated, or immaterial.

issues.legal_issue: A demand for independent proof of the precise times of last seeing the accused with the deceased and discovering the death is not decisive where eyewitnesses establish the killing and the events occur within a short period.
material_facts: Witnesses testified to the altercation and strangulation, and other witnesses testified to the subsequent loading of the body parts for disposal.
The events occurred within a short period around midnight, although witnesses differed slightly about the times.
The accused offered no reasonable or plausible explanation for what happened to the deceased after they were seen with him.
issues.conclusion: The time-related challenge to the last-seen evidence failed; the evidence supported the finding that the accused were responsible for the murder.
issues.legal_principle: The last-seen inference requires reasonable temporal proximity between the accused and deceased being seen alive together and the deceased being found dead; where the gap is so small that another perpetrator becomes an impossible possibility, the inference may arise. The accused may then be expected to explain what happened. The principle is fact-dependent (S.K. Yusuf v. State of West Bengal; Mohd. Azad @ Samin v. State of West Bengal; State v. Mahender Singh Dahiya). Here, eyewitness evidence of the killing made independent proof of the precise times unnecessary.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and eyewitnesses_saw_killing and events_occurred_within_short_period and accused_offered_no_plausible_explanation

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.eyewitnesses_saw_killing: Witnesses testified to seeing the killing.
predicates.events_occurred_within_short_period: The relevant events occurred close enough in time to support the prosecution’s account.
predicates.accused_offered_no_plausible_explanation: The accused gave no reasonable explanation for what happened after they were seen with the deceased.

issues.definition: Where eyewitnesses saw the killing, the events were close in time, and the accused offered no plausible explanation, a challenge based on the absence of independent proof of precise times does not defeat the guilt inference.

issues.legal_issue: Identification in court may support a conviction despite the absence of identification at a test identification parade when the identification evidence is otherwise reliable and corroborated.
material_facts: One accused was not identified by a witness at the identification parade.
That witness was not examined at trial, and the court did not rely on his recorded statement.
Several other witnesses identified the accused in court, and the court found their identifications reliable.
issues.conclusion: The failure to identify the accused at the parade was inconsequential and did not undermine the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The Code of Criminal Procedure does not require an identification parade. Such a parade is an investigative tool, and identification at the parade is corroborative of identification in court. Identification in court for the first time is not ordinarily a sufficient basis for conviction without corroboration, but that is a rule of prudence subject to exceptions (Munshi Singh Gautam v. State of M.P.; Sheo Shankar Singh v. State of Jharkhand).

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and identification_parade_not_supportive and reliable_court_identification and identification_corroborated_by_other_evidence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.identification_parade_not_supportive: A test identification parade did not identify the accused or otherwise support the prosecution identification evidence.
predicates.reliable_court_identification: Witnesses reliably identified the accused in court.
predicates.identification_corroborated_by_other_evi: Other evidence supports the identification of the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, an unsuccessful or absent parade identification does not defeat a conviction when reliable in-court identification is supported by other evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Joint criminal liability applies when several persons participate in a criminal act in furtherance of their common intention, which may develop at the scene.
material_facts: The accused had jointly demanded money and threatened the deceased if he did not comply.
Witnesses placed the accused together during the altercation and killing, and evidence showed their collective involvement in strangling the deceased and disposing of his body.
The court found that the accused’s presence and actions demonstrated common intention and collective participation.
issues.conclusion: The accused were liable for the murder through joint participation in furtherance of their common intention.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires a criminal act by several persons and a common intention shared by them; participation in the joint act must be established. It creates constructive liability, so each participant may be liable for the ultimate criminal act even if each did not perform the same act or inflict a fatal injury. Common intention may arise at the scene and is inferred from the facts and circumstances (Nand Kishore v. State of Madhya Pradesh; Lallan Rai v. State of Bihar; Dharnidhar v. State of Uttar Pradesh; Jai Bhagwan v. State of Haryana).

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and multiple_persons_participated_in_criminal_act and shared_common_intention and acts_furthered_shared_purpose

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.multiple_persons_participated_in_crimina: More than one person participated in the criminal act.
predicates.shared_common_intention: The participants shared an intention to bring about the criminal purpose.
predicates.acts_furthered_shared_purpose: The participants’ acts furthered their shared criminal purpose.

issues.definition: When multiple participants act in furtherance of a shared criminal purpose, each may be held liable for the criminal act carried out through their joint participation.
